pages.title: Teacher Resources Overview
pages.html:
TEACHER-FACING · DO NOT SHARE WITH STUDENTS
Teacher Resources

This module is unpublished and visible only to teachers. It collects everything you need to run College Counseling & Critical Thinking. Keep it unpublished so students never see it.

What's here

  • Teacher Manual (PDF) — the full facilitator reference: how the course works, the intro/outro wrappers, AI & VR guidance, gradebook setup (55/25/15/5 weighting), rubrics for every graded item, weekly announcement scripts, a workload map, an adaptation guide for live 4-day-a-week sections, and the complete standards-coverage crosswalk.
  • Editable Syllabus (Word .docx) — a teacher-editable syllabus with bracketed fields for your name, office hours, and dates. Customize it in Word, then post or share it however your program prefers. A student-facing version is also live on the course Syllabus page.

Semester scope

This Canvas course is Semester 1 (Modules 1-3, the course's Quarter 1). Modules 4-6 (Money, Applying, College Essay, including the five-step Resume project) are built and will deploy as Semester 2.

Two deploy-time items flagged in the manual: before each cycle, verify the current Common App essay word limit (Module 6) and the current Bright Futures CLT concordance / Common App prompts (Module 5), since those change yearly.

assignments.title: Net Price & Funding Plan
assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
COLLEGE COUNSELING & CRITICAL THINKING
Quarter / Module
Q2 · Module 4
Paying for College
Lesson
Lesson 4.03
Focus
Net Price & Funding Plan
One real college, one real plan
Points
Assignment
25 pts
Lesson 4.03
Net Price & Funding Plan
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
A real number and a realistic plan to cover it
Built from your work in Lessons 4.01 through 4.03
You will run the official net price calculator for one real college you are genuinely considering, then build an Excel spreadsheet that shows how you would realistically cover that net price: which funding sources, in what order, and how much from each. This is not a fantasy budget. It is a first working draft of the money plan you will refine in Module 5, and your teacher will respond to it like a counselor, not a grader.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
For one college you actually care about: what would it really cost your family, and where, specifically, would the money come from?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Pick one real target college. Choose a school you are genuinely considering (your Module 3 list is a good source). Find its net price calculator: search the college's name plus "net price calculator," or use the Department of Education's directory at collegecost.ed.gov.
2
Run the calculator. For your own family planning, sit down with a parent or guardian and use real numbers privately. For the version you submit, protect your family's privacy: enter $0 for all family financial information and note that your submitted result is the privacy-protected estimate. Record the school's cost of attendance and the calculator's net price output.
3
Build your spreadsheet in Excel (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account). Save it to OneDrive as LastName_NetPriceFundingPlan. You may start from the course's Optima_College_Budget_Template.xlsx or build your own. Include three sections: (a) Costs: the cost of attendance broken into tuition, fees, room and board, and books/personal; (b) Net price: the calculator's estimate and the grants/scholarships it assumed; (c) Funding plan: a line for each realistic source (specific scholarships you could pursue, work-study or a job, family contribution, savings, and loans last) with an estimated dollar amount for each, totaling to the net price.
4
Make the funding lines specific. "Scholarships: $5,000" is a wish. "Bright Futures (state merit): est. $3,000; two local community scholarships from my tracker: est. $1,000 each" is a plan. Use your scholarship notes from Lesson 4.02, and the Optima_Scholarship_Tracker_Template.xlsx if you want a ready-made structure for the scholarship lines.
5
Add a short reflection in a text box or final rows of the spreadsheet (4 to 6 sentences): What surprised you about the net price? Which funding source are you least sure about? If a loan appears in your plan, why is the amount you chose the right amount and not more?
🔒 YOUR FAMILY'S PRIVACY IS PROTECTED
You are never required to share your family's income or finances with your teacher or classmates. Run the calculator with real numbers privately for your own planning; submit the $0-entry version. Your plan is graded on the quality of its reasoning and realism, not on your family's numbers.
⚠️ USE REAL SOURCES FOR REAL NUMBERS
An AI tool can help you set up spreadsheet formulas or check your math. It cannot give you this college's current costs or aid: those must come from the college's own net price calculator and website. Any dollar figure an AI quotes for a specific school is unverified. Every number in your submitted plan should trace to a source you actually opened.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The spreadsheet names one real college and records its cost of attendance and an actual net price calculator result.
☐
Costs are broken into the four components from Lesson 4.01, and the funding plan totals to the net price.
☐
Funding sources are specific and follow the order of operations: free money first, earned money second, loans last and only for the remaining gap.
☐
The reflection honestly names what surprised you and what is least certain in the plan.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Understanding of costs
7 pts		 Real calculator result recorded; costs correctly broken into components; sticker vs net clearly understood. Result recorded; minor gaps in the breakdown. Costs partly guessed or lumped together. No real calculator result. 7 pts
Quality of reasoning
6 pts		 Funding sources are specific, realistic, and follow free-earned-borrowed order; loan amount (if any) is justified. Mostly specific; order mostly followed. Generic lines ("scholarships") without specifics. Plan does not connect to the net price. 6 pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All three spreadsheet sections plus the reflection; funding lines total to the net price. Minor gaps. Several gaps or totals do not reconcile. Largely incomplete. 6 pts
Clarity & honesty
6 pts		 Spreadsheet is readable and labeled; reflection names real surprises and uncertainties. Clear, mostly honest reflection. Hard to follow or reflection is generic. Unclear or missing reflection. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Net Price & Funding Plan
Upload your Excel spreadsheet (.xlsx) from OneDrive. Keep this file. You will update it in Module 5 when you build your full college-research spreadsheet.
Due: by the end of Module 4.
A rough but honest plan beats a polished fantasy. If a number is a guess, label it a guess; your teacher can help you replace guesses with facts.

Lesson 5.01
College Application Tracker
Assignment · 10 pts (completion)
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
One spreadsheet that turns a pile of deadlines into a page you control
Built from your work in Lesson 5.01
Applications are lost far more often to missed deadlines than to weak essays. In this assignment you build a single Excel spreadsheet that holds every requirement, fee, and due date for the colleges you are considering. You will keep updating it through senior year, so build it to last.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If every application deadline lived in one place, what would you need to see at a glance to never miss one?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In Excel (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account), create a new spreadsheet. Save it to your OneDrive and name it LastName_ApplicationTracker. If you like, start from the Optima College Budget or Scholarship Tracker templates provided in this course.
2
Make one row for each college you are seriously considering (at least 4). If you are early in the process, use realistic candidates from your Module 3 shortlist.
3
Add a column for each of these: application platform (Common App, direct, or state system); application deadline and type (early or regular); application fee, or a note if a fee waiver applies; required tests and scores; essays or supplements required; recommendation letters required; scholarship deadlines; and a status column.
4
Fill in what you can find from each college's admissions website. Leave a cell blank rather than guessing, and mark cells you still need to research.
💡 WHERE AI CAN HELP, WITH A CATCH
An AI tool can help you draft the column headers or summarize a college's requirements. It can also state a deadline confidently and be wrong. Always confirm every date and fee against the college's own admissions page. A missed deadline caused by a bad AI answer is still a missed deadline.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
At least four colleges, one per row.
☐
All required columns are present and mostly filled from real sources.
☐
The sheet is readable at a glance, and unresearched cells are marked, not guessed.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: College Application Tracker
Upload your Excel file (.xlsx) from OneDrive. This is graded on completion, so a genuine, usable tracker earns full credit. Keep it open all year and update it as deadlines firm up.
Due: by the end of Module 5.

assignments.title: Resume Step 1 Check-In: Brainstorm Your Material
assignments.html:
Submit the brainstorm from your project document:

  1. Your accomplishments list: at least 12 items, drawn from work, leadership, service, school, skills, and unique interests. Start from your Module 1 Personal Stock Inventory and grow it.
  2. Your wish list: 2 to 3 areas you wish you could add this year (volunteer work, a leadership role, a job, a skill), each with one concrete action you could take toward it.

This is checked for completion, not graded for polish. Write fast, judge later.

assignments.title: Resume Step 2 Check-In: Read Your Audience
assignments.html:
Submit three things from your project document:

  1. Your target: the one real college, scholarship, or job this resume is written for.
  2. Your evidence list: at least 10 key words and preferred qualifications collected from your target's website and materials.
  3. Your five-minute freewrite describing your target's ideal candidate. Unedited is fine; that is what a freewrite is.

assignments.title: Resume Step 3 Check-In: Find the Overlap
assignments.html:
Submit your marked-up comparison from your project document: at least 5 overlap items, each pairing one of your real accomplishments with the audience word or priority it matches (word matches and idea matches both count).

If your honest overlap came up thinner than 5, submit what you found plus one sentence naming the gap you plan to close this year. A thin overlap honestly named is a complete submission.

assignments.title: Resume Step 4 Check-In: Rough Draft
assignments.html:
Upload your complete rough-draft resume as a Word document (.docx):

  • All sections your material fills (Contact, Education, Experience, Activities & Service, Skills & Interests).
  • Overlap content placed first, then your best remaining accomplishments.
  • Bullets written (action verb + what you did + scope or result).

It does not need to look good yet. Formatting and layout are Step 5's job.

assignments.title: Resume Step 5 Check-In: Design Pass
assignments.html:
Submit two things:

  1. Your resume draft laid out on one page, with your strongest content in the top-left area.
  2. Three design decisions, each explained in one sentence: what you changed and why (for example, what you cut to reach one page, what you moved into the prime position, what you did to make the page easier to skim).

assignments.title: Resume Pitch Recording
assignments.html:
Read your resume's opening section aloud, then record yourself delivering it as a spoken 60-second pitch, the way you would introduce yourself to an interviewer or an admissions interviewer. Look at the camera or speak clearly into the microphone; this is about practicing your own voice and pacing, not about production quality.

Submit the recording (audio or video, your choice) using Canvas's built-in recorder or an uploaded file. This is checked for completion: did you actually record and submit a real spoken pitch in your own words, not read in a flat monotone straight off the page.

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online

Project
Resume Project · Final
Focus
Your Polished One-Page Resume
Built through Steps 1–5
Points

25 pts
Resume Project · Final Deliverable
Final Resume
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
The polished, one-page resume you built across Steps 1 through 5
A document you can actually use, this year, for a real audience
This is the finished product of the Resume Project: one page, written for the real target you chose in Step 2, filled with your overlap content first, and designed so a skimming reader catches your strongest material. Your teacher will read it the way a real reviewer would and give you feedback you can apply to every future version of this document.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If your reader gives this page fifteen seconds, what will they remember about you, and is that what you want them to remember?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
In Word (through your Optima Microsoft 365 account), finalize your resume from Step 5. Save it to your OneDrive and name it LastName_Resume.
2
Confirm the content. Your overlap material (Step 3) leads, your best remaining accomplishments round it out, and every line is true and specific enough to talk about in an interview.
3
Confirm the design. One page exactly. Strongest content in the top-left area. One font, consistent sizes, aligned dates, real white space. Mature and grounded; any touch of personality is tasteful and purposeful.
4
Proofread twice. Read it aloud once for errors. Then ask someone to skim it for thirty seconds and tell you what they remember; if they miss your strongest item, adjust its placement before you submit.
5
Add a two-sentence note at the top of your submission comments (not on the resume itself): who your target audience is, and which item you placed in the prime top-left position and why.
⚠️ POLISH, NOT PRODUCE
Spell check and formatting tools are fair game for polish. The content, the choices, and the wording need to be yours, because you are the one who will be asked about every line of this page in interviews and college visits. A resume you built yourself is one you can defend without hesitation.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Exactly one page, with your strongest overlap content leading in the top-left area.
☐
Content clearly matches your chosen target's key words and preferred qualifications.
☐
Bullets are specific, active, and honest; every line could survive a follow-up question.
☐
The page is easy to skim, consistently formatted, and free of errors.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Audience fit
7 pts		 Content clearly matches the target's priorities; overlap material leads the page. Mostly matched; overlap mostly prominent. Generic; little connection to the target. No evident audience. 7 pts
Quality of content
6 pts		 Bullets are specific, active, and honest, with scope or results named. Mostly specific and active. Vague or passive in places. Thin, vague, or inflated. 6 pts
Design & readability
6 pts		 One page; skimmable; strongest content in prime position; mature and grounded. Clean with minor placement or spacing issues. Crowded, thin, or hard to skim. Over a page or visually chaotic. 6 pts
Clarity & correctness
6 pts		 Error-free; consistent formatting and punctuation throughout; own voice. A few small inconsistencies. Several errors or inconsistencies. Frequent errors; clearly unproofed. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Final Resume
Upload your Word document (.docx) from OneDrive, and add your two-sentence target-and-placement note in the submission comments.
Due: by the end of Module 5.
Keep this file and update it as you add experiences. A resume is a living document, and the next version will take you a fraction of the time now that you know how it is built.

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company

The College Essay
Lesson
Lesson 6.05
Focus
Final College Essay
Draft, feedback, required revision
Points
Assignment
25 pts
Lesson 6.05
Final College Essay
Assignment · 25 pts · the course capstone
📖 WHAT THIS ASSIGNMENT IS
The essay you have been building toward all semester
Angle, story, reflection, drafted in full and revised
You found an angle, learned to tell the story, built it to a reflection, and studied the real prompts. Now you write the whole essay, submit it for your teacher's feedback, and complete a required revision. Revision is not a formality here. It is where a good essay becomes a strong one.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Does this essay sound like you, and only you, and does it show a reader how you think?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Choose one Common Application prompt (from Lesson 6.05) that fits the angle you developed. In Word (Microsoft 365), create LastName_CollegeEssay saved to OneDrive. At the top, type the prompt you chose.
2
Write the full essay: open with a crisp narrative moment or a bold claim, tell your true story with concrete detail, and build to a reflection that shows how you think and decide. Stay within the prompt's word limit (the main Common App essay is 250 to 650 words; confirm the current limit on the Common App site).
3
Submit the full draft for your teacher's feedback.
4
Required revision: read your teacher's feedback carefully, revise the essay, and submit the improved version. The revision is graded.
⚠️ THIS ESSAY MUST BE YOURS
AI-generated essays are not accepted. Beyond the honesty issue, they defeat the purpose: the point is to think through your own life and say it in your own voice, which is exactly what interviews and visits will ask of you. A tool may check spelling on work that is already yours. It cannot have your experiences or your judgment.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
One true story, chosen to fit a real prompt, carries the whole essay.
☐
It shows your thinking and decisions, not just events or other people.
☐
Clear, specific prose in your own voice, within the word limit.
☐
The revision responds to your teacher's specific feedback.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (4) Proficient (3) Developing (2) Beginning (1) Pts
Angle & story
7 pts		 One vivid, true story carries the whole essay. Clear story; some focus drift. Story is thin or generic. No clear story. 7 pts
Insight & reflection
6 pts		 Shows real thinking, decisions, and growth. Some reflection. Mostly events, little insight. No insight. 6 pts
Craft & clarity
6 pts		 Strong opening, concrete detail, clean prose, within the word limit. Mostly clear; minor issues. Unclear or padded. Hard to follow. 6 pts
Authenticity & honesty
6 pts		 Unmistakably your own voice; honest and specific; revision responds to feedback. Mostly own voice; some revision. Generic feel; thin revision. Not your voice; no revision. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Final College Essay
Submit your Word document (.docx) from OneDrive for the first draft. After your teacher's feedback, submit your revised version to the same assignment. Both submissions are expected; the revision is graded.
Due: draft and revision deadlines are posted in Module 6. Leave real time between them.

Finding scholarships and grants that fit me

questions.text: How confident do you feel about understanding college costs today? (1 = not at all, 5 = very)
Have you and your family talked about how college might be paid for?
A college's cost of attendance includes:

answers.text: Tuition, fees, room and board, books, and personal costs

questions.text: The sticker price of a college is:

answers.text: The published cost of attendance, before any aid is subtracted
The price after grants and scholarships

questions.text: The net price is:

answers.text: The same for every student at a school
What a specific family pays after grants and scholarships are subtracted
Always higher than the sticker price

questions.text: A college with a higher sticker price always costs a family more than a college with a lower sticker price.
At public universities, out-of-state students typically pay:

answers.text: The same tuition as in-state students
Considerably more than in-state students, often two to three times as much

answers.text: Room, board, books, and personal costs

answers.text: Scholarships and grants first, earned money second, loans last

questions.text: Match each source to its type.

questions.text: If a family doubts they will qualify for need-based aid, filing the FAFSA is a waste of time.

answers.feedback: Some aid is not need-based, some colleges require the FAFSA for merit scholarships, and federal loans require it.

questions.text: The main advantage of a Direct Subsidized Loan over an unsubsidized one:

answers.text: It never has to be repaid
The government pays the interest while you are in school and during the grace period

answers.text: Every college that participates in federal student aid programs, on its website

questions.text: Your aid offer includes a larger loan than your actual funding gap. Borrowing wisely means:

answers.text: Accepting only the amount you need and declining the rest
Accepting the full amount as a cushion

discussions.title: Sticker Shock Discussion
discussions.html:
After Lesson 4.01 you looked up the published cost of attendance for one college. Share: (1) the college and its sticker price, (2) one thing inside that number that surprised you (a fee, room and board, the size of the total), and (3) your reasoning about whether the net price for a typical aided student might be meaningfully lower, using what you learned about grants, scholarships, and aid. Keep it to about 4-6 sentences. Do not share any of your family's financial information.

Then reply to one classmate whose college has a very different sticker price from yours. What might explain the difference: school type, location, in-state versus out-of-state, or something else? If their reasoning about sticker-vs-net used a step yours did not, name it: comparing how someone else worked the same problem is one of the fastest ways to sharpen your own numbers.

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
Real numbersNames a real college and its actual published cost of attendanceVague or unsourced figureAbsent
ReasoningExplains the sticker-vs-net logic with a specific observationAsserts without supportAbsent
Reply to a classmateSubstantive: proposes a real explanation for the price differenceThin ("Wow, expensive!")Absent

discussions.title: Which Test Fits You? Discussion
discussions.html:
Based on Lesson 5.03, which admissions test (SAT, ACT, or CLT) would you most likely take, and why? Point to one specific feature of the test and one thing about your own strengths or target colleges that supports your choice. Keep it to about 4-6 sentences. If you would apply test-optional, make that case instead.

Then reply to one classmate whose choice differs from yours. What is one fair point in their reasoning?

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
Names a test/choice with a specific test featureSpecific and accurateVagueAbsent
Ties the choice to own strengths or target collegesClear connectionAsserted onlyAbsent
Reply to a classmateSubstantive, fair-mindedThinAbsent

discussions.title: Essay Angles Discussion
discussions.html:
In a few sentences, share the angle you chose for your essay: the one true story or idea, and what you hope it shows a reader about you. Do not write the essay here, just the angle.

Then reply to one classmate. Name the one moment or detail in their angle you would most want to hear more about, and why it caught your attention.

CriterionFull (2)Partial (1)Missing (0)
States a clear, specific angleOne focused story/ideaVague or several unfocused ideasAbsent
Says what it should revealConnects story to a trait/insightAsserted onlyAbsent
Reply to a classmateSpecific, encouraging, usefulThin ("nice idea")Absent
